newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb generals contest dismissals.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb generals contest dismissals.

text.p: Purged generals of the Bosnian Serb army (BSA) claimed on Sunday they were still in command with the support of all ranks.
Sources in the high command sacked by President Biljana Plavsic told Reuters that a new army commander and a deputy who replaced General Ratko Mladic and senior aides were unqualified lightweights.
"Not a single BSA officer -- let alone the (dismissed) generals -- have offered them any support," a general staff source said.
"The headquarters staff remains in control of the entire BSA. All commanders at all levels are informing us that they recognise only our command."
The source did not say how the sacked generals, who survived a similar attempt by the civilian leadership to oust them last year, would tackle Plavsic's challenge.
She swore in General Pero Colic to replace Mladic, an indicted war criminal, on Sunday and General Dragan Josipovic as his deputy in an effort to seal civilian control over the post-war army.

Plavsic blamed international pressure for the move but diplomats said it was probably convenient for her to get rid of Mladic, an aggressive commander who political leaders found hard to control during the 1992-95 war against Bosnian Moslems and Croats.
The headquarters source sneered at Colic as a former colonel pulled out of retirement and Josipovic as never having undergone advanced military studies.

Colic hit back saying that the new commanders were combat-tested and told reporters: "The basis of this new general staff is that we proved ourselves on the battlefield -- we're not armchair generals."
Diplomats said Plavsic's purge also suited Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in his quest to show the West he is cooperating with the Bosnian peace process.
Milosevic, whose government steered and funded the Bosnian Serb army, once used the military to force obedience from Bosnian Serb political leaders who opposed concessions in peace negotiations.
Western envoys have also made clear to Serb leaders that reconstruction aid will depend on adhering to the peace treaty, which bars Mladic and other war crimes suspects from holding public office.
Despite public bluster, Mladic has tended to obey the wishes of his superiors in Belgrade.
With the army facing serious financial difficulties, and with health problems of his own, a low-profile retirement may be an attractive escape.
Preparing the ground for his departure, Belgrade media with ties to the government have cast doubt on his health and predicted his retirement for the past several weeks.

The dismissal illustrated a shift in the balance of power between the Bosnian Serb army and civilian authorities since wartime civilian leader Radovan Karadzic tried and failed to sack Mladic last year.
With the end of the Bosnian war a year ago, the Serb police -- under the command of civilian leaders -- has become the dominant force in Bosnia's Serb republic.
The army has been plagued by morale problems, desertion, and a lack of financial support since the tide of war turned in favour of their Moslem-Croat foes.
It was the second major change in Serb leadership since July, when Karadzic bowed to international pressure and stepped down as president.
Both Mladic and Karadzic have been indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
